If someone is stingy, it means they are unwilling to give, spend, or share — even when they can easily afford to. A stingy person holds on tightly to what they have and gives as little as possible to others.

The key thing to understand is this: stingy is never about being unable to give. It is always about being unwilling to give. If a poor person can't afford to buy you a gift, that's not being stingy — that's simply not having enough money. But if a wealthy person refuses to leave a decent tip at a restaurant, or counts every single grape before sharing, or haggles over a tiny amount just to avoid spending — that is being stingy.
What stingy feels like in real life

Imagine you go out to dinner with a friend who earns a good salary. When the bill comes, he pretends to check his phone. When you split the check, he quietly leaves out his share of the tax. At the end, he leaves a 2% tip. You walk out thinking, "Wow, he's so stingy."

Or think of a boss who never gives raises, never buys the team coffee, and reuses paper clips obsessively — not because the company is struggling, but simply because parting with anything feels painful to her. That's stingy.

This is important: you can be stingy with anything that can be given or shared — not just money.

  • A person can be stingy with compliments — they rarely tell you that you did a good job, even when you clearly did.
  • A chef can give you a stingy portion — a tiny, barely-there serving of food.
  • A manager can be stingy with praise — they never acknowledge hard work.
  • Someone can be stingy with their time — always too busy to help, even for five minutes.

In all these cases, the idea is the same: they have enough to give, but they give as little as they possibly can.

Stingy is not a neutral word. It carries a strong negative judgment. When you call someone stingy, you are not just describing their behavior — you are criticizing it. You're saying they should be giving more, and their refusal to do so is selfish and ungenerous. People don't like being called stingy, and for good reason — it implies a kind of emotional smallness, a coldness toward others.
How stingy is different from similar words

This is where many learners get confused, so pay close attention.

Frugal and thrifty are often mistaken for stingy, but they are very different — and actually positive words. A frugal person is careful and smart with money. They avoid waste, look for good deals, and don't spend on things they don't need. But when it truly matters — when a friend needs help, when a bill must be paid, when a gift is appropriate — a frugal person spends without a problem. Frugal is wise. Stingy is selfish.

Cheap is close to stingy and often used in everyday speech to mean the same thing. It's a bit more casual and blunt. "Cheap" can sometimes also mean low quality (a cheap product), but when used about a person ("He's so cheap"), it means essentially the same as stingy.

Miserly is the extreme version of stingy. A miser is almost obsessively attached to their money and possessions — think of the classic image of Ebenezer Scrooge in A Christmas Carol, who let people around him suffer in poverty while he hoarded his wealth. Stingy is bad; miserly is worse.

Generous is the direct opposite of stingy. A generous person gives freely and happily, without keeping score.
How to use "stingy" in a sentence

You'll most commonly see stingy used in these two patterns:

"He/She is stingy with [something]."
→ She is stingy with her time.
→ The restaurant is stingy with portions.

Or simply before a noun:
→ He's a stingy person.
→ That was a stingy raise — only 1% after two years of hard work.
→ Don't be stingy — give him a proper helping.

Knowing the other forms of the word will help you recognize it anywhere:

The noun is stinginess — "His stinginess made everyone uncomfortable at dinner."
The adverb is stingily — "She stingily poured just a drop of sauce onto the plate."
A stingy person is sometimes called a miser, a cheapskate, or a tightwad in informal English.
A stingy person has enough to give — they just don't want to.
